 Two tennis players of Vietnamese origin both entered the world's top 20.
 Learner Tien and Brandon Nakashima are both among the top 20 male tennis players in the world, following remarkable career advancements. Behind these two American tennis representatives are family stories with Vietnamese roots.
 Báo Tuổi Trẻ • 22/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e Add Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e 0 Learner Tien (left) and Nakashima are prominent tennis players of Vietnamese origin - Photo: LAVER
 According to the ATP rankings released earlier this week, Brandon Nakashima is ranked 17th with 2,375 points, just above Learner Tien, who is ranked 18th with 2,345 points. This is not the first time these two players of Vietnamese origin have entered the top 20, but it is the first time they have been ranked side-by-side in such a remarkable position.
 The breakthrough of the young talent of Vietnamese origin. 
 Separated by five years in age and both growing up in California, the two players took different paths to reach the top of the world rankings.
 For Tien (20 years old), it's the rapid rise of a young talent. For Nakashima (25 years old), his current success also signifies a comeback after injury and a period of decline.
 Learner Tien was born on December 2, 2005, in Irvine to parents who immigrated from Vietnam to the United States. His father, Khuong, is a lawyer; his mother, Huyen, is a teacher.
 The name Learner, meaning "learner," was chosen after his mother's profession. His sister's name, Justice, is associated with their father's work.
 Tien's tennis journey began when he accompanied his father to the court. Mr. Khuong started by giving his son the ball to practice hitting, and later became his first tennis instructor.
 Starting from a family tennis career, Tien entered the U.S. Tennis Association's junior program at around age 10, and subsequently won the U18 national championship twice in a row in 2022 and 2023. He studied for a semester at the University of Southern California before turning professional in 2023.
 In 2024, a rib injury sidelined Tien for about three months. Upon his return, he won 28 consecutive matches in the ITF and Challenger series, securing three Challenger titles in the latter half of the season.
 Those initial steps led the left-handed player to a turning point at the 2025 Australian Open: qualifying, defeating Daniil Medvedev in a nearly five-hour match, and advancing to the round of 16.
 You may also like In November 2025, Tien won his first ATP Tour title in Metz, France, after defeating Cameron Norrie. A month later, he beat Alexander Blockx to win the Next Gen ATP Finals, the season-ending tournament for the best young players. 
 Learner Tien is expected to boom in 2026 - Photo: REUTERS
 From a player who had to seek opportunities in lower-level tournaments, Tien has now won titles that confirm his abilities on a bigger stage.
 The 2026 season continued his progress. At the Australian Open, Tien once again eliminated Medvedev, this time with a convincing 6-4, 6-0, 6-3 victory to reach his first Grand Slam quarterfinal. He became the youngest male player to reach the quarterfinals of the tournament since Nick Kyrgios in 2015.
 Under the guidance of former Roland Garros champion Michael Chang, Tien further expanded his competitiveness on clay courts. In May, he defeated Mariano Navone in the Geneva final to win his second ATP Tour title. This victory made Tien the youngest American male player to win an ATP Tour tournament on European clay courts since 1989.
 Reaching the Indian Wells quarterfinals, the Montreal semifinals, and the round of 16 at the US Open further added to this year's outstanding season.
 Returning after injury 
 While Tien grew up in a family where both parents were from Vietnam, Nakashima's Vietnamese ancestry comes from her mother's side.
 His mother, Christina, was born in Vietnam and moved to California as a child; his father, Wesley, is Japanese-American. Both are pharmacists. As a child, Nakashima often played softball with his maternal grandfather, who was one of the people who introduced him to tennis early on.
 Born on August 3, 2001, in San Diego, Nakashima attended the University of Virginia and was honored as the ACC Rookie of the Year in 2019 before turning professional.
 2022 marked his first major breakthrough: winning the ATP Tour in his hometown of San Diego, reaching the round of 16 at Wimbledon, and winning all five matches to claim the Next Gen ATP Finals title in Milan. 
 You may also like Nakashima is in excellent form - Photo: ATP
 But that upward trajectory was halted in 2023. A left knee injury sidelined Nakashima for nearly two months, and his ranking plummeted from its peak of 43 to outside the top 150. He returned to Challenger tournaments to regain his rhythm and confidence, gradually rebuilding his position on the ATP Tour.
 By the summer of 2026, his perseverance paid off. Nakashima reached his first Masters 1000 final in Montreal, after defeating Rafael Jodar in the semi-finals. Although he lost to Ben Shelton in the final, he continued his form by reaching the semi-finals in Cincinnati shortly afterwards. These two crucial results propelled him into the top 20 in the world rankings.
 Under coach Wayne Ferreira, Nakashima had a consistent season, finishing as runner-up in Brisbane and reaching the semi-finals of Acapulco, Queen's Club, and Washington, ultimately achieving his highest career ranking.
